# Summarizing by Hand



Functions that automate your descriptive statistics tables for you (e.g., the amazing [gtsummary package](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/index.html)) inevitably entail some level of compromise. It is unreasonable for a single function to anticipate the diversity of needs out there. Sometimes you need a table to be a particular way, and you need to do the heaving lifting yourself. After all that, the `apa_flextable` function will get a flextable table close to APA style. You may need to do some additional styling with flextable as well.

The flextable package helper functions for automating summary tables. The `tabulator`, `summarizor`, and `proc_freq` functions are particularly powerful ways of summarizing and describing data. However, I am going to compute my summaries with standard base R and tidyverse functions. Here I create a table of means, standard deviations, and sample sizes for several variables across groups. The particulars are not so important here, just that apa7 and flextable can do most of the rest after that. 

```{r dataprocessing}
d <- ggplot2::diamonds %>% 
  select(cut, price, carat, depth, table) %>% 
  arrange(cut) %>% 
  rename_with(str_to_title) %>% 
  pivot_longer(where(is.numeric), names_to = "Variable") %>% 
  summarise(
    M = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(Variable, Cut)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(c(M, SD)) %>% 
  unite(Variable, Variable, name) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = Variable) 
```

The `apa_flextable` function handles most of the formatting automatically except for the dollar signs, which flextable can add later. @tbl-apaflextable also decimal aligns all the numbers, though this is apparent in column `n` only.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-apaflextable
#| tbl-cap: Price, Carat, Depth, Table Using `apa_flextable`
d |> 
  apa_flextable() |> 
  colformat_char(j = 3:4, prefix = "$") 

```


# Automatic Summaries with the `apa_descriptives` Function

The first table of most empirical papers describes the sample. `apa_descriptives` makes this table: for each continuous variable, its mean and standard deviation, *M* (*SD*), and for each categorical variable, the number and percentage of respondents at each level, *n* (%). Numeric variables are treated as continuous, and factors, character vectors, and logical vectors as categorical. Each categorical variable has a heading row, with its levels indented below it.

## The Whole Sample

The `survey` data set in the MASS package has the answers of 237 statistics students to a short questionnaire. Without groups, there is one column for the whole sample:

```{r}
#| label: survey
d_survey <- MASS::survey |> 
  mutate(Exer = fct_recode(Exer, Frequently = "Freq") |> fct_relevel("Frequently", after = Inf),
         Smoke = fct_recode(Smoke, Occasionally = "Occas", Regularly = "Regul") |> fct_relevel("Heavy", after = Inf))



apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  variables = c("Age", "Height", "Pulse", "Smoke", "Exer"),
  labels = c(
    Height = "Height (cm)",
    Pulse = "Pulse (beats per minute)",
    Smoke = "Smoking",
    Exer = "Exercise"
  )
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

Variables are named by their formatted names unless `labels` gives better ones. Percentages are of the non-missing responses, and the note lists the number of missing values of each variable that has any.

## Groups

With `by`, each group gets a column, with its size in the header, followed by a column for the whole sample (`total = FALSE` leaves it out). Rows whose group is missing are left out, and the note says how many.

```{r}
#| label: survey-by-sex
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  variables = c("Age", "Height", "Pulse", "Smoke", "Exer"),
  by = "Sex",
  labels = c(
    Height = "Height (cm)",
    Pulse = "Pulse (beats per minute)",
    Smoke = "Smoking",
    Exer = "Exercise"
  )
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Skewed Variables and Group Differences

Age is strongly skewed in this sample (most students are about 20, a few much older), so its median and interquartile range, *Mdn* (*IQR*), describe it better. `continuous` sets the description of particular variables.

With `test = TRUE`, a *p* column tests the group differences: Welch's *t* test (two groups) or Welch's one-way ANOVA (more groups) for variables described by their mean, the Kruskal–Wallis test for variables described by their median, and the chi-square test of independence for categorical variables. When a categorical variable's table has an expected count below 5, where the chi-square approximation is poor, Fisher's exact test is used for that variable instead, and the note names it (`categorical_test = "chisq"` or `"fisher"` uses one test for all categorical variables). Tests are not shown by default, because many journals discourage testing baseline differences in randomized trials, where any difference is due to chance.

```{r}
#| label: survey-tests
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  variables = c("Age", "Height", "Pulse", "Smoke", "Exer"),
  by = "Sex",
  continuous = c(Age = "median_iqr"),
  test = TRUE,
  labels = c(
    Height = "Height (cm)",
    Pulse = "Pulse (beats per minute)",
    Smoke = "Smoking",
    Exer = "Exercise"
  )
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Missing Values and Ranges

By default, the note lists the missing values. With `missing = "row"`, each variable with missing values gets a "Missing" row with the number of missing values in each column instead. With `range = TRUE`, each continuous variable gets a "Range" row with its minimum and maximum:

```{r}
#| label: survey-missing-range
apa_descriptives(
  d_survey,
  variables = c("Height", "Pulse", "Smoke"),
  by = "Sex",
  missing = "row",
  range = TRUE,
  labels = c(
    Height = "Height (cm)",
    Pulse = "Pulse (beats per minute)",
    Smoke = "Smoking"
  )
) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)
```

## Options

* `categorical` treats numeric codes (e.g., 1 = yes, 0 = no) as categories.
* `digits` and `percent_digits` set the decimal places of the statistics and the percentages.
* `format_variable_names = FALSE` keeps unlabeled variable names exactly as they are.

For tables with other layouts, see the [article on summarizing data](summarize.html), which builds a table step by step with flextable.
